flashcards.definition: The legacy firmware that initializes the motherboard's components so the OS can load; its setup program uses the keyboard arrow keys, and most boards now use UEFI instead.
The firmware most motherboards now use in place of BIOS, adding 64-bit CPU operation, a GUI with mouse support, networking at boot, and better boot security.
The boot sequence, or boot device priority: the order in which the firmware searches devices such as the fixed disk, USB, optical drive, or network for a boot manager.
A boot option that starts the computer from the network: its network adapter retrieves boot instructions from a configured server.
A firmware security setting that enables or disables individual USB ports or all of them, since USB connections can pose security risks.
Firmware fan settings: a mode (Balanced, Cool, Quiet, Fanless, or Custom), the minimum temperature at which the fans start, and a duty cycle, where a higher percentage runs them faster.
Viewing temperatures such as the CPU's, either in the BIOS/UEFI monitoring or sensors entry or in a third-party app that can alert when a safe limit is passed.
A password required before the OS loads; the user (system) password locks the whole computer until it is entered, so everyone who uses the PC must know it.
The supervisor, administrator, or setup password, which restricts access to the BIOS/UEFI setup program.
A UEFI feature that protects against malware by checking the OS bootloader against pre-loaded keys and refusing to run one that is unsigned or modified.
Hardware that securely stores cryptographic keys, such as BitLocker's, and checks the firmware and boot loader for tampering; it can be enabled, disabled, or reset in BIOS/UEFI setup.
Hardware that securely stores cryptographic keys, such as a secure USB key that unlocks with a password, PIN, or fingerprint; useful when a PC has no TPM or its TPM is damaged.
Front-panel LEDs are off and no fans can be heard; the cause may be the PSU, the incoming electricity, the power cable or connectors, or a fuse.
The diagnostic program in the system firmware that checks the hardware needed to boot; it runs once the CPU gets the power good signal from the PSU.
Beep codes that report a POST error when the fault keeps anything from showing on screen; look up what a code means on the manufacturer's website.
If the fans run but nothing shows and no beeps sound, it is likely a display problem or POST is not running.
How each OS shows a serious crash: a blue screen (BSOD) in Windows, a spinning pinwheel in macOS, and a kernel panic in Linux.

reference.title: Troubleshoot OS Errors and Crash Screens

flashcards.definition: The Windows crash screen, caused by faulty or incompatible drivers, corrupted system files, defective hardware, or overheating or power supply issues; scan its QR code for details.

reference.title: Troubleshoot OS Errors and Crash Screens

flashcards.definition: When a PC suddenly turns off, power problems are a common cause; if it happens only after the PC has run a while, suspect heat.
A system hot to the touch that may crash or reboot; check the temperature sensors, CPU fan, heat sink and thermal paste, blanking plates, and the room.
A smell of burning or smoke from the PC, which usually means overheating, most likely in the power supply (dust-clogged vents can also cause it); shut the system down at once.
Bulging capacitors on the motherboard, a visible sign of damage or a manufacturing defect; confirm the problem with diagnostic software.
Check for overheating first, since heat makes the CPU throttle, then for a misconfiguration after any change, then test each subsystem against a baseline.
If the clock is wrong in system setup, the RTC battery may be failing; replace it with a battery of the same type.
The coin-cell lithium battery, usually a CR2032, that keeps the real-time clock running while the PC is off; often called the CMOS battery.
The firmware finds nothing to boot from and halts; check the drive's power, data cable, and UEFI/BIOS settings, then suspect file corruption or a faulty drive.
Loud grinding, clicking, or scraping from a hard disk drive, which often means mechanical failure (a healthy HDD makes only a low-level noise); back up the data immediately and replace the drive.
Drive lights: none lit can mean the system or drive has no power, or a RAID array is missing or failed, and a red LED usually marks a failed disk.

Nonstop drive activity, seen as constant drive LED activity; it could mean the system has too little RAM, causing excessive paging to the disk, or a faulty software process, malware, or a failing disk.
If File Explorer does not show a drive, check that it is initialized, partitioned, and formatted; if Disk Management cannot see it, suspect hardware or cables.
Warning sounds from enterprise drives or RAID controllers when a drive or array fails or a drive goes missing from an array; they need immediate attention.
The self-diagnostic program built into most fixed disks, which can alert the operating system when it detects a failure.
Slow reads and writes; run drive diagnostics, since failing sectors (HDD) or blocks (SSD) can cause it, as can heavy app load, HDD fragmentation, or low free space.
A drive performance statistic that counts input/output (read and write) operations per second, reported by diagnostic tests; a result below the vendor's baseline means the drive is likely faulty.
Files that cannot be opened or that disappear, often because they sit on failing sectors (HDD) or blocks (SSD); on an HDD with no backup, try a recovery utility.

One disk in a redundant array fails: the volume is listed as degraded but still works, so replace the disk soon and rebuild; if more disks fail than the array can tolerate, or the controller fails, the volume goes missing.
No image because the monitor is set to the wrong port, such as an empty DVI port instead of the HDMI port in use; choose the input in the OSD.
The monitor's own menus, worked by buttons on its case, for choosing the input source and adjusting brightness, color, contrast, and power saving.
A loose, stretched, or crimped video cable, or one not rated for the job (4K needs a High-Speed HDMI cable); test by swapping in a known-good cable.
A completely failed projector bulb, which may pop and show scorch marks or a broken filament; let the projector cool fully before replacing it.
A projector that turns itself off from time to time, usually from overheating; check its fan, clear and unblock its vents, and check the room temperature, then look for loose cables or a loose bulb.
Raise brightness and contrast in the OSD and check power-saving or adaptive brightness modes; if the image is barely visible, the backlight may have failed.
A blurry picture, often because the output resolution does not match the display's native resolution; set the right resolution in the OS or update the video driver.
The monitor's own resolution, such as 1920x1080, that the computer's output should match; a mismatch makes the image fuzzy or the wrong size.
Check that the video cable is securely attached; flickering can also come from a failing backlight or internal circuitry, or a faulty or overheating video card.
Flat-panel pixels that stay black, unlike stuck pixels that stay bright; they usually cannot be repaired, so check the warranty for a replacement.
A ghost image left when a static image stays on screen too long, more common on OLED and plasma; prevent it with a screen saver or auto-off.
Calibrate the display with a color profile in the Color Management applet; purple or green lines or sudden color changes often mean a bad connector or cable.
DVI and VGA carry no audio, unlike HDMI and DisplayPort; also check the speakers' power, connections, and volume, and the audio output selected in the OS.
The picture is the wrong size for the screen, with black bars around the edges or an image stretched to fill it; set the native resolution, fit the image with the OSD, and update the video driver.
The picture looks wavy or bent out of shape, such as a pincushion effect; check for interference from nearby electronics, secure the cables, and match the monitor's native resolution.
